payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Homework at the Garden Fence

[1] Every Thursday evening this fall, a few cars have been parked along the fence of the Hollis Creek Community Garden with their engines off and their dome lights on. [2] Inside them are kids from up on Marrow Ridge doing homework, because the weak Wi-Fi from the garden shed reaches the gravel lot and their houses get no signal at all. [3] Internet is important for students these days.

[4] My name is Tessa Lindqvist, and I was one of those kids last spring. [5] Our teachers post every assignment online, and the county's math program will not even load on a phone showing one bar. [6] My neighbor's son, Caleb, failed a chemistry quiz because the practice set timed out four times on his mother's hotspot. [7] Obviously, anyone who doesn't get this is clueless about how school works now.

[8] The garden committee could fix part of this problem cheaply. [9] A signal booster mounted on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, according to the hardware co-op in Pell. [10] A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would let students work somewhere other than a cold car. [11] The garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours would be needed.

[12] Some members worry that teenagers will trample the beds or leave trash behind. [13] Students using the table would agree to stay by the shed and to pick up before leaving each night. [14] I am asking every member to vote yes at the November 9 meeting.

el_passage.title: Homework at the Garden Fence
paragraphs: Every Thursday evening this fall, a few cars have been parked along the fence of the Hollis Creek Community Garden with their engines off and their dome lights on.
Inside them are kids from up on Marrow Ridge doing homework, because the weak Wi-Fi from the garden shed reaches the gravel lot and their houses get no signal at all.
Internet is important for students these days.
My name is Tessa Lindqvist, and I was one of those kids last spring.
Our teachers post every assignment online, and the county's math program will not even load on a phone showing one bar.
My neighbor's son, Caleb, failed a chemistry quiz because the practice set timed out four times on his mother's hotspot.
Obviously, anyone who doesn't get this is clueless about how school works now.
The garden committee could fix part of this problem cheaply.
A signal booster mounted on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, according to the hardware co-op in Pell.
A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would let students work somewhere other than a cold car.
The garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours would be needed.
Some members worry that teenagers will trample the beds or leave trash behind.
Students using the table would agree to stay by the shed and to pick up before leaving each night.
I am asking every member to vote yes at the November 9 meeting.

issues.issue: The stray header line 'ALTON original passage' is production metadata and should be removed from the student-facing text.
The hardware co-op in Pell and the 140-dollar figure are fictional local details, which is fine for an invented flyer, but the cost claim is not tied to any verifiable source.

Sentence 5 is flagged in the blueprint as the place to acknowledge older members who studied without internet. The sentence as written is a plain statement about assignments being online, so the omission is present but subtle for students to spot.

Sentence 7 is intentionally insulting ('clueless'), so the flaw is clear. The flyer's audience is the voting members, and the sentence does insult readers who may not 'get this', so it works as the planned tone flaw.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Draft: Why Transfer Night Matters

[1] Every spring, the second-floor meeting room at the Harlan Ferry Public Library fills with folding chairs, a dented coffee urn, and people who are not sure they belong there. [2] Community college is a good thing for a lot of people. [3] Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors from Calloway Valley Community College and two state universities to answer questions one at a time.

[4] Last year I met a man named Arturo Pell, who had left high school at seventeen to work in his uncle's tire shop. [5] At forty-one, he had just finished an associate degree at Calloway Valley, and he was trying to figure out which of his credits would count toward the nursing program at Ridgeline State University. [6] An advisor spent twenty minutes with him going over a printed transfer agreement, the sheet listed every Calloway Valley course that Ridgeline would accept. [7] He left with a plan and a highlighted copy of that sheet folded into his jacket pocket.

[8] Arturo's story is not unusual. [9] Many students start at community colleges because tuition is lower, because classes meet at night, or because they need time to rebuild confidence after a rough start somewhere else. [10] Transfer pathways are basically like a whole bunch of agreements and stuff that colleges make so that what you learn at one place gets counted at another place, which is really important. [11] Without them, a returning student can lose a semester or more retaking classes he or she has already passed.

[12] Anyway, that is pretty much what the night is about. [13] Hope to see you there.

paragraphs: Every spring, the second-floor meeting room at the Harlan Ferry Public Library fills with folding chairs, a dented coffee urn, and people who are not sure they belong there.
Community college is a good thing for a lot of people.
Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors from Calloway Valley Community College and two state universities to answer questions one at a time.
Last year I met a man named Arturo Pell, who had left high school at seventeen to work in his uncle's tire shop.
At forty-one, he had just finished an associate degree at Calloway Valley, and he was trying to figure out which of his credits would count toward the nursing program at Ridgeline State University.
An advisor spent twenty minutes with him going over a printed transfer agreement, the sheet listed every Calloway Valley course that Ridgeline would accept.
He left with a plan and a highlighted copy of that sheet folded into his jacket pocket.
Arturo's story is not unusual.
Many students start at community colleges because tuition is lower, because classes meet at night, or because they need time to rebuild confidence after a rough start somewhere else.
Transfer pathways are basically like a whole bunch of agreements and stuff that colleges make so that what you learn at one place gets counted at another place, which is really important.
Without them, a returning student can lose a semester or more retaking classes he or she has already passed.
Anyway, that is pretty much what the night is about.
Hope to see you there.

blueprint.purpose: To announce the library's annual Transfer Night and persuade adult readers, especially those returning to school, that community college transfer pathways offer a real second chance

ALTON original passage
The Silent Player: Watching a Conductor at Work

[1] Conductors are interesting and there are many things to say about them. [2] For our music-history project, I spent three Thursday rehearsals watching Maestra Ilse Okonkwo-Dahl lead the Corlett Valley Youth Orchestra. [3] She is the only person on the stage who makes no sound at all.

[4] Before the first rehearsal, the principal cellist told me that the musicians follow the conductor's breath more closely than her baton. [5] At the second rehearsal, I watched Okonkwo-Dahl inhale sharply just before the opening chord of the overture the group was learning, and all forty players came in together. [6] Later, when she forgot to breathe before the same chord, the entrance was ragged.

[7] Conductors always control everything that happens in a performance. [8] In the third rehearsal, Okonkwo-Dahl stopped the brass section four times in ten minutes. [9] Honestly, the brass guys got kind of bossed around, but she never raised her voice. [10] She just lowered her left hand slowly, and the trumpets got softer, which was a thing that happened each time she did the hand thing, and it was pretty awesome to see.

[11] In the end, conductors are a big deal.

ALTON original passage
Forty Lengths at Harrow Street

[1] Every summer since I was fourteen, I have spent my mornings at the Harrow Street Pool in Calder Falls, first as a swimmer and now as a lifeguard. [2] Pools are important to communities in many ways.

[3] At six in the morning, the lap lanes belong to retirees like Mr. Okafor, who swims exactly forty lengths and then tells me the water temperature as if I had not measured it myself. [4] By noon, the shallow end fills with day-camp kids whose counselors call out names in four languages. [5] The pool brings together people who would never otherwise meet. [6] Last July, I watched a retired machinist teach a nine-year-old girl from the apartments on Delmont Avenue how to float on her back, his hand flat beneath her spine until she no longer needed it.

[7] Last spring, the city council proposed closing Harrow Street to save money. [8] Everyone in town agreed that this was a terrible idea. [9] I spoke at the budget hearing, holding a petition with 312 signatures I had collected at the snack bar. [10] The council kept the pool open, but it cut the evening hours, the only time many working parents could bring their children. [11] That decision was totally lame, and honestly it bugged me a lot.

[12] What I learned from all of this is that the thing I learned is that a public space only stays public if the people who use it are willing to show up and speak up for it in the places where the decisions about it get made. [13] In conclusion, swimming is a very good form of exercise for people of all ages.

issues.issue: Sentence 2 ('Pools are important to communities in many ways.') is a vague, stock-sounding filler sentence that is not among the planned flaws. It weakens the opening and reads as AI-generic. Consider cutting it or making it specific, though it is tolerable in a draft.

Sentence 12 repeats itself ('What I learned from all of this is that the thing I learned is that...'). This matches the planned concision flaw (8.B), so it is intentional. Noting that the repair should cut the duplicated clause and tighten the long tail.

The planned flaws at sentences 5, 8, 10, 11, 12 and 13 are all present and detectable: unsupported claim (5), overstated 'Everyone agreed' (8), missing transition or causal link between the council keeping the pool open and cutting evening hours (10), slangy 'totally lame... bugged me' (11), wordy repetition (12), and off-purpose conclusion about exercise (13). Sentence 10's flaw is subtle, since 'but' already supplies some contrast, but the missing cause-effect link is arguable and acceptable.

Sentence 6 already gives a strong specific example of strangers connecting, which slightly undercuts the planned flaw at sentence 5. The flaw is still valid, because sentence 5 itself is an unsupported generalization placed before the anecdote. Revisers should note that the evidence is partly present just after the claim.
